title: A galaxy on the edge
caption: The edge-on galaxy NGC 4762, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 4762 · constellation Virgo · about 60 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A bright streak slices across this Hubble image. It is the galaxy NGC 4762, seen edge-on, and scattered in the background are a number of other, far more distant galaxies.

Found in the constellation of Virgo, NGC 4762 lies about 58 million light-years from us. It belongs to the Virgo Cluster, which sits at the center of the larger Virgo supercluster, the same supercluster that contains our own Local Group of galaxies.

Astronomers once thought NGC 4762 was a barred spiral. It has since been identified as a lenticular galaxy, a type that sits between an elliptical and a spiral. Seeing it edge-on makes its true shape hard to judge, but astronomers have identified four main parts to it, which are a bulge at the center, a bar, a thick disc and a ring on the outside. Its disc is lopsided and warped, perhaps because it once swallowed a smaller galaxy whose remains settled into the disc and rearranged its gas and stars.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.52 x 2.52 arcminutes) and distance (60 million light years), the frame spans roughly 44,000 × 44,000 light-years. Its light set out about 60 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, combining visible (475 nm) and near-infrared (850 nm) filters. The colors assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light used here is invisible to the eye, and Hubble's long exposures reveal background galaxies far too faint to see.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: The galaxy is also listed as VCC 2095 in the Virgo Cluster Catalog, which covers just over 2000 galaxies. It hosts a LINER-type active galactic nucleus, a very energetic central region identified by particular spectral lines that act like atomic fingerprints, revealing what the region is made of.
alt: A thin, bright streak of an edge-on galaxy slicing across the frame, with small faint galaxies scattered in the background.
